units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
MRS. ARBUTHNOT appears on terrace behind .
For the world has been made by fools that wise men should live in it!
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Enter L.C. LADY HUNSTANTON and DR. DAUBENY.

Ah! here you are, dear Lord Illingworth. Well, I suppose you have been telling our young friend, Gerald, what his new duties are to be, and giving him a great deal of good advice over a pleasant cigarette.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I have been giving him the best of advice, Lady Hunstanton, and the best of cigarettes.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I am so sorry I was not here to listen to you, but I suppose I am too old now to learn. Except from you, dear Archdeacon, when you are in your nice pulpit. But then I always know what you are going to say, so I don’t feel alarmed.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Sees MRS. ARBUTHNOT.
Ah! dear Mrs. Arbuthnot, do come and join us. Come, dear.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Enter MRS. ARBUTHNOT.
Gerald has been having such a long talk with Lord Illingworth; I am sure you must feel very much flattered at the pleasant way in which everything has turned out for him. Let us sit down.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: They sit down .
And how is your beautiful embroidery going on?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I am always at work, Lady Hunstanton.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Mrs. Daubeny embroiders a little, too, doesn’t she?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: She was very deft with her needle once, quite a Dorcas. But the gout has crippled her fingers a good deal. She has not touched the tambour frame for nine or ten years. But she has many other amusements. She is very much interested in her own health.
units.name: THE ARCHDEACON

units.text: Ah! that is always a nice distraction, is it not? Now, what are you talking about, Lord Illingworth? Do tell us.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I was on the point of explaining to Gerald that the world has always laughed at its own tragedies, that being the only way in which it has been able to bear them. And that, consequently, whatever the world has treated seriously belongs to the comedy side of things.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Now I am quite out of my depth. I usually am when Lord Illingworth says anything. And the Humane Society is most careless. They never rescue me. I am left to sink. I have a dim idea, dear Lord Illingworth, that you are always on the side of the sinners, and I know I always try to be on the side of the saints, but that is as far as I get. And after all, it may be merely the fancy of a drowning person.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: The only difference between the saint and the sinner is that every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Ah! that quite does for me. I haven’t a word to say. You and I, dear Mrs. Arbuthnot, are behind the age. We can’t follow Lord Illingworth. Too much care was taken with our education, I am afraid. To have been well brought up is a great drawback nowadays. It shuts one out from so much.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I should be sorry to follow Lord Illingworth in any of his opinions.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: You are quite right, dear.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: GERALD shrugs his shoulders and looks irritably over at his mother .
Enter LADY CAROLINE.
Jane, have you seen John anywhere?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: You needn’t be anxious about him, dear. He is with Lady Stutfield; I saw them some time ago, in the Yellow Drawing-room. They seem quite happy together. You are not going, Caroline? Pray sit down.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I think I had better look after John.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Exit LADY CAROLINE.

It doesn’t do to pay men so much attention. And Caroline has really nothing to be anxious about. Lady Stutfield is very sympathetic. She is just as sympathetic about one thing as she is about another. A beautiful nature.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Enter SIR JOHN and MRS. ALLONBY.
Ah! here is Sir John!
And with Mrs. Allonby too!
I suppose it was Mrs. Allonby I saw him with.
Sir John, Caroline has been looking everywhere for you.
We have been waiting for her in the Music-room, dear Lady Hunstanton.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Ah! the Music-room, of course. I thought it was the Yellow Drawing-room, my memory is getting so defective.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: To the ARCHDEACON.
Mrs. Daubeny has a wonderful memory, hasn’t she?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: She used to be quite remarkable for her memory, but since her last attack she recalls chiefly the events of her early childhood. But she finds great pleasure in such retrospections, great pleasure.
units.name: THE ARCHDEACON

units.text: Enter LADY STUTFIELD and MR. KELVIL.
Ah! dear Lady Stutfield! and what has Mr. Kelvil been talking to you about?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: About Bimetallism, as well as I remember.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Bimetallism! Is that quite a nice subject? However, I know people discuss everything very freely nowadays. What did Sir John talk to you about, dear Mrs. Allonby?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: About Patagonia.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Really? What a remote topic! But very improving, I have no doubt.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: He has been most interesting on the subject of Patagonia. Savages seem to have quite the same views as cultured people on almost all subjects. They are excessively advanced.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: What do they do?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Apparently everything.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Well, it is very gratifying, dear Archdeacon, is it not, to find that Human Nature is permanently one.—On the whole, the world is the same world, is it not?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON
